scope_note: One pass with two lenses after edit: claims (unsupported-claim hunter) and technical (senior SA red team); the lens is named in each type. Ran 'saa.py sync 11' first (written=0 unchanged=12). Read 1-fast.md, 2-deep.md, 3-do.md, 4-say.md, 5-quiz.md (10 shipped questions), sources.md, data/11-vpc-connectivity/{questions,tasks,speak,cards}.json (incl. the verified spares q003 and q011) and the diagram specs vpc-connectivity-hero/before/after. Refutation attempts that held (no finding): peering quota 50 / up to 125 and 168-hour request expiry; full mesh 4,950; TGW quotas 5 / 5,000 / 20 and 100 Gbps per VPC attachment per AZ each direction; endpoint bandwidth 10 to 100 Gbps; $0.01/GB cross-AZ peering; static route beats propagated route; most specific route first (blackhole /24 inside a propagated /16); AZ without an attachment subnet cannot reach the TGW; pending-acceptance route is a blackhole (t02); default endpoint policy is full access (t03); aws:PrincipalAccount with Principal * in a gateway endpoint policy (docs/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3 has that exact example); s3express is a Gateway service name (t01); describe-vpc-endpoint-services filters owner and service-type exist; aws:SourceIp does not work through an S3 endpoint; inter-Region peering cannot reference security groups (FAQ and docs/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-security-groups); removing endpoint-service permissions keeps accepted connections; allow-everyone plus accept-all makes the load balancer public; NAT gateway cannot be reached through peering; NACL allow and deny vs security group allow only; cross-Region interface endpoints for AWS services on 2025-11-19 (examinable); story numbers match STARTUP.md (bank and prod 10.20.0.0/16, dev 10.40.0.0/16, network 10.60.0.0/16).

findings.quote: > **Try it:** Limit a gateway endpoint to one bucket and watch other buckets refuse. See [3-do.md](3-do.md). <!-- task: vpc-connectivity-t03 -->
findings.evidence: Task vpc-connectivity-t03 (data/11-vpc-connectivity/tasks.json) creates no instance and sends no S3 request: its steps are get-caller-identity, describe-availability-zones, create-vpc, describe-route-tables, create-vpc-endpoint, two describe-vpc-endpoints reads of PolicyDocument and one modify-vpc-endpoint; verify is describe-vpcs. The reader can never 'watch other buckets refuse'. Step 8 itself only says requests 'stop passing the endpoint after a few minutes', which the task does not observe (vpc-endpoints-policy-update-takes-minutes, docs/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-access: "After you update an endpoint policy, it can take a few minutes for the changes to take effect."). The tasks note in the ledger states the break-it was changed to 'observe the default policy'. Rewrite the callout to what the task does, for example: 'See the default full-access endpoint policy, then narrow it to one bucket. See [3-do.md](3-do.md).'

findings.quote: | Through a third network? | No: [transitive peering relationships are not supported](../facts/vpc-peering.md#vpc-peering-faq-not-transitive) | Yes: [all attachments can route packets to each other](../facts/transit-gateway.md#transit-gateway-centralized-router-scenario) | No |
findings.evidence: The PrivateLink cell 'No' has no fact link, and a verified fact of this chapter says the opposite for traffic that arrives through another network: privatelink-wp-endpoints-reachable-over-peering-tgw-dx, docs/whitepapers/latest/building-scalable-secure-multi-vpc-network-infrastructure/aws-privatelink: "You can access AWS PrivateLink endpoints over VPC peering, VPN, Transit Gateway, Cloud WAN, and AWS Direct Connect." 2-deep.md answers 'Yes' to a peered VPC using an interface endpoint, FAQ 5 answers 'Yes' for Direct Connect, and shipped question q010 keys an interface endpoint reached from the data center through Direct Connect and a transit gateway. A reader who memorizes this cell will reject that key. Rephrase the row (for example 'Joins the networks so traffic can pass through?') or change the cell to 'Yes, to the endpoint only' with the fact link above.

findings.quote: | "one service for VPCs with the same CIDR" | an endpoint service | VPCs [can have overlapping IP address ranges](../facts/privatelink.md#privatelink-wp-consumer-and-provider-may-overlap) | both sides start connections: renumber, then peering |
findings.evidence: The 'But not if' cell has no fact and suggests an in-place fix that AWS does not offer. vpc-cidr-cannot-resize, docs/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-cidr-blocks: "You cannot increase or decrease the size of an existing CIDR block." A secondary non-overlapping block does not help either: vpc-peering-no-overlap-even-if-unused-cidr, docs/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics: "If you have multiple IPv4 CIDR blocks, you can't create a VPC peering connection if any of the CIDR blocks overlap, even if you intend to use only the non-overlapping CIDR blocks or only IPv6 CIDR blocks." Renumbering means building a new VPC and migrating, which is never the low-effort answer. The chapter's own verified spare q011 keys the documented alternative: a second endpoint service in the other direction (privatelink-faq-consumer-initiates-allowlisted-customers, privatelink-endpoint-service-needs-load-balancer). Suggested cell: 'both sides start connections: a second endpoint service the other way'.

findings.quote: Yes: [all attachments can route packets to each other](../facts/transit-gateway.md#transit-gateway-centralized-router-scenario)
findings.evidence: The quote is true only in the centralized-router configuration. transit-gateway-centralized-router-scenario, docs/vpc/latest/tgw/how-transit-gateways-work: "In this scenario, all attachments are associated with the transit gateway default route table and propagate to the transit gateway default route table. Therefore, all attachments can route packets to each other". 2-deep.md subsection 4 teaches that separate route tables block traffic between groups (transit-gateway-isolated-vpcs-blocked-no-route). Card vpc-connectivity-c008 states the condition correctly. Suggested cell: 'Yes, when they share a route table: [all attachments can route packets to each other]'.

findings.quote: | What you pay | [Data transfer across peering connections is charged](../facts/vpc-peering.md#vpc-peering-faq-no-creation-charge) | Hourly: the [connections that you make to the Transit Gateway](../facts/transit-gateway.md#transit-gateway-pricing-hourly-attachment-and-data-processing), plus traffic | Endpoint hours [provisioned in each Availability Zone](../facts/privatelink.md#privatelink-faq-billing-interface-gwlb-hourly-per-az) |
findings.type: claims: incomplete-pricing (also 2-deep.md step 4 'Pay' and speak s02)
findings.evidence: (1) Peering: the FAQ line reads as 'all peering data is charged', but a verified fact of this chapter gives the exception: vpc-peering-guide-pricing-no-creation-charge-free-in-az, docs/vpc/latest/peering/what-is-vpc-peering: "All data transfer over a VPC peering connection that stays within an Availability Zone is free, even if it's between different accounts. Charges apply for data transfer over VPC peering connections that cross Availability Zones and Regions." The same simplification is in 2-deep.md subsection 2 step 4 ('data transfer across peering connections is charged') and speak vpc-connectivity-s02 ('Creating a peering connection is free. You pay for data transfer across it.'). (2) PrivateLink: only hours are named while the TGW cell adds 'plus traffic'; privatelink-faq-billing-data-processing-per-gb, www/privatelink/faqs: "Data processing charges apply for each gigabyte processed through the VPC endpoints, regardless of the traffic’s source or destination." A cost comparison built on this row is skewed both ways.

findings.quote: 2. **Resolve.** With **private DNS**, applications reach the endpoint [without requiring that you make any changes](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-interface-private-dns-no-app-change).
findings.evidence: The fact's qualifier is 'the VPC has both DNS hostnames and DNS resolution enabled', and the sentence drops it. vpc-endpoints-interface-private-dns-no-app-change, docs/vpc/latest/privatelink/privatelink-access-aws-services: "If you enable private DNS for your interface VPC endpoint, and your VPC has both DNS hostnames and DNS resolution enabled, we create a hidden, AWS-managed private hosted zone for you." 'Endpoint created, but the application still resolves the public address' is a common troubleshooting stem whose answer is these two VPC attributes. Add 'when the VPC has DNS hostnames and DNS resolution turned on'.

findings.quote: Yes. Unlike a **gateway endpoint**, you can [access AWS PrivateLink endpoints over VPC peering](../facts/privatelink.md#privatelink-wp-endpoints-reachable-over-peering-tgw-dx).
findings.evidence: True at the network level, but the next subsection teaches private DNS, and private DNS does not carry over a peering connection. docs/vpc/latest/peering/vpc-peering-basics (VPC peering limitations): "You cannot connect to or query the Amazon DNS server in a peer VPC." docs/vpc/latest/privatelink/privatelink-access-aws-services: "The Route 53 Resolver automatically resolves local VPC domain names and record in private hosted zones. However, you can't use the Route 53 Resolver from outside your VPC." Instances in VPC B that call the service's default name go to the public endpoint, not to the endpoint in VPC A. One clause fixes it: 'Yes, through the endpoint-specific DNS name' (vpc-endpoints-faq-onprem-dx-dns-returns-private-ip).

findings.quote: > **Exam signal:** "a few VPCs, the lowest latency and cost" points to peering, with the [lowest overall cost and highest aggregate performance](../facts/vpc-peering.md#vpc-peering-wp-lowest-cost-highest-performance).
findings.evidence: Exam signal is strict after its quoted phrase (CONVENTIONS-2 decision 33), and the signal claims 'lowest latency', which no linked fact says. vpc-peering-wp-lowest-cost-highest-performance, docs/whitepapers/latest/building-scalable-secure-multi-vpc-network-infrastructure/vpc-peering: "VPC peering offers the lowest overall cost and highest aggregate performance when compared to other options for inter-VPC connectivity." Aggregate performance is throughput, not latency. Change the quoted phrase to 'a few VPCs, the lowest cost and highest throughput', or ground latency in a fact.

findings.quote: | [$0.01/GB in both "In" and "Out" direction](../facts/vpc-peering.md#vpc-peering-cross-az-data-transfer-price) | Peering traffic between zones | Busy peers belong in one zone |
findings.evidence: 'Busy peers belong in one zone' is a design rule with no fact, and it pushes the reader toward a single-AZ design that the chapter warns against: vpc-endpoints-interface-two-azs-for-production, docs/vpc/latest/privatelink/privatelink-access-aws-services: "Configure at least two Availability Zones per VPC endpoint and deploy your AWS resources that must access the AWS service in these Availability Zones." Shipped question q009 also requires the design to 'stay in three Availability Zones'. The cost fact behind the rule is verified but not linked: vpc-peering-cross-az-data-transfer-price, display 'stays within an Availability Zone is free'. Suggested cell: 'Same-zone peering traffic [stays within an Availability Zone is free]; weigh it against resilience.'

findings.quote: It [does not override or replace IAM user policies](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-wp-one-policy-per-endpoint-no-override), so the role needs its own allow.
findings.evidence: In the same account an allow in the bucket policy is enough, even when the role's identity policy allows nothing. iam-eval-identity-policy-no-allow-is-implicit-deny, docs/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic_policy-eval-denyallow: "Depending on the type of principal, an `Allow` in a resource-based policy can result in a final decision of `Allow`, even if an implicit deny in an identity-based policy, permissions boundary, or session policy is present." The linked fact's own second half names bucket policies: "An endpoint policy does not override or replace IAM user policies or service-specific policies (such as Amazon S3 bucket policies)." The table above says 'The table assumes no bucket policy'; the trap does not. Suggested: 'so the role still needs an allow from its IAM policy or the bucket policy'.

findings.quote: 2. **Narrow.** You [attach a single endpoint policy to the endpoint](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-policy-single-policy-default-if-none) that names the buckets. It [must contain a Principal element](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-policy-json-iam-language-principal-required).
findings.evidence: The subsection's scenario is an S3 gateway endpoint, and for a gateway endpoint the Principal element cannot name the role. vpc-endpoints-policy-gateway-principal-star-use-principalarn, docs/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-access: "With gateway endpoints, the `Principal` element must be set to `*`. To specify a principal, use the `aws:PrincipalArn` condition key." The prose never says it, but shipped question q006 (option 'Change the Principal element ...') and task t03 step 7 both depend on it. Add: 'For a gateway endpoint, Principal stays * and a condition names the principals.'

findings.quote: "expect": "The new policy: the example bucket as Resource, Principal *, and a Condition with your account ID. Requests for other buckets stop passing the endpoint after a few minutes."
findings.evidence: After the Fix-it step the only check reads back the policy document the reader just wrote, so it cannot fail, and the effect claimed in its second sentence is never observed (see claims-01). A no-instance check that proves the endpoint is in the path is possible: describe-route-tables on $RTB_ID shows a route whose GatewayId is the vpce- ID (docs/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3: "We automatically add a route that points traffic destined for the service to the endpoint network interface."). Say plainly that the denial can be seen only from an instance in the VPC. Also add one sentence before the reader copies the policy: this one-bucket policy blocks every other bucket for every instance in the VPC, including AWS-owned buckets such as package repositories (vpc-endpoints-faq-benefit-restrict-users-actions-resources).

findings.quote: | "isolate VPC groups on one transit gateway" | separate route tables | you segment by [creating multiple route tables](../facts/transit-gateway.md#transit-gateway-faq-route-tables-segment) | traffic needs inspection: an inspection VPC |
findings.evidence: 'an inspection VPC' has no fact and no definition anywhere in the chapter (lint W901 flags the term), and inspection is not an alternative to segmentation: an inspection design still uses separate transit gateway route tables, with the inspection VPC as a shared service. transit-gateway-wp-centralize-shared-services, docs/whitepapers/latest/aws-vpc-connectivity-options/aws-transit-gateway: "centralize access to shared services such as traffic inspection, interface VPC endpoint access, or egress traffic through a NAT gateway or NAT instances." Either link that fact and write 'traffic between groups needs inspection: add an inspection VPC as a shared service', or choose a true 'but not if'.

findings.quote: The 40 TB then flows over the peering connection instead of the transit gateway, and there is [no charge for creating VPC peering connections](../facts/vpc-peering.md#vpc-peering-faq-no-creation-charge).
findings.evidence: The stem's charge is per-GB transit gateway data processing on 40 TB a month; a creation charge does not explain the saving, and the sentence lets the reader infer the 40 TB becomes free. The supporting facts are verified and unused: transit-gateway-pricing-data-processing-per-gb-sent-to-gateway, www/transit-gateway/pricing: "Data processing charges apply for each gigabyte sent from a VPC, Direct Connect or VPN or Network Firewall to the AWS Transit Gateway (1 gigabyte = 1024 megabytes)."; vpc-peering-guide-pricing-no-creation-charge-free-in-az: "Charges apply for data transfer over VPC peering connections that cross Availability Zones and Regions." Name the per-GB processing charge that peering does not have, and that cross-zone peering traffic is still charged.

findings.quote: "answer": "Yes. Share it with AWS Resource Access Manager, across accounts or across your organization. An account that gets an invitation must accept the resource share first."
findings.evidence: The CTO asks about 'our other accounts'; inside an organization with RAM sharing turned on there is no invitation. ram-org-sharing-no-invitations, docs/ram/latest/userguide/getting-started-sharing: "When you share resources in your organization, AWS RAM doesn't send invitations to principals. Principals in your organization gain access to shared resources without exchanging invitations." Spoken aloud, the answer suggests a manual accept step for every account. Suggested: 'Inside your organization, with sharing turned on, there is no invitation; an account outside it must accept one first.'

findings.quote: > **Changed recently:** (2025-11-19) Cross-Region interface endpoints.
findings.evidence: Two verified changes since mid-2022 that touch this chapter's core choices have no Changed recently note. (1) dynamodb-change-privatelink-interface-endpoints-2024-03, docs/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/DocumentHistory: "Amazon DynamoDB now supports AWS PrivateLink. With AWS PrivateLink, you can simplify private network connectivity between virtual private clouds (VPCs), DynamoDB, and your on-premises data centers using interface VPC endpoints and private IP addresses. ... | March 19, 2024". Older exam questions assume DynamoDB has only a gateway endpoint, while shipped q009 option b already relies on DynamoDB interface endpoints. (2) privatelink-change-cross-region-access-2024, docs/vpc/latest/privatelink/doc-history: "Cross-Region access | A service provider can host a service in one Region and make it available in a set of AWS Regions. A service consumer selects a service Regions when creating an endpoint. | November 26, 2024" (endpoint services, the Callvale and bank pattern; the chapter's only scope statement is the whitepaper's 'within an AWS Region' in privatelink-wp-only-consumer-initiates).

findings.quote: Nothing here yet.

findings.section: vpc-connectivity-q011 option d (verified spare, not shipped)
findings.quote: "why": "It works, because private NAT gateways [enable communication between networks even if they have overlapping CIDR ranges](../facts/vpc.md#vpc-private-nat-allow-listed-and-overlapping), but it adds gateways to run."
findings.type: technical: wrong-mechanism ('works' distractor that does not work as written)
findings.evidence: Option d says private NAT gateways 'translate the overlapping addresses of the callback traffic' with both VPCs on a transit gateway. The documented design needs routable secondary ranges and a load balancer on the receiving side, not NAT alone. docs/vpc/latest/userguide/nat-gateway-scenarios (Enable communication between overlapping networks): "Each VPC has its original IP address range, which is non-routable, plus the routable IP address range assigned to it by the IP management team. VPC A has a subnet from its routable range with a private NAT gateway. ... VPC B has a subnet from its routable range with an Application Load Balancer." A transit gateway also does not route identical CIDRs (transit-gateway-faq-identical-cidr-not-routed). q011 is not in 5-quiz.md now, but it is the spare for a twin swap; fix the why before it can ship.

findings.quote: 4. **Reach from outside.** The endpoint is [accessible from on-premises networks over VPN](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-wp-interface-endpoints-reachable-from-onprem) and Direct Connect.
findings.evidence: The same fact sentence continues with the DNS step that makes the service's normal name work from on premises: vpc-endpoints-wp-interface-endpoints-reachable-from-onprem, docs/whitepapers/latest/building-scalable-secure-multi-vpc-network-infrastructure/centralized-access-to-vpc-private-endpoints: "Use conditional forwarding rules to send all DNS traffic for the full-service endpoint names to Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoints, which will resolve DNS requests according to the private hosted zone." Without it, on-premises clients must use the endpoint-specific DNS names (vpc-endpoints-faq-onprem-dx-dns-returns-private-ip), as q010 does. One clause is enough.

findings.quote: 3. **Combine.** The role's IAM policy and the bucket still decide.
findings.evidence: A behavior claim without a fact link in a how-it-works step. The verified fact is vpc-endpoints-policy-does-not-override-identity-or-resource-policies, docs/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-access: "An endpoint policy does not override or replace identity-based policies or resource-based policies." Link it (display 'does not override or replace identity-based policies') and say 'the bucket policy', not 'the bucket'.

findings.quote: | Leaves the bucket out | Allows the read | Denied |
findings.evidence: The only Denied row without a reason or link. Supported by vpc-endpoints-faq-benefit-restrict-users-actions-resources, www/privatelink/faqs: "When accessing Amazon services over VPC endpoints, you can restrict the access through a VPC endpoint to specific users, actions, and/or resources." Link it as the row above links the implicit deny.

findings.quote: | Reach from a peered VPC or the data center | No: it [cannot be extended out of a VPC](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-gateway-not-extended-past-vpc) | Yes |
findings.evidence: The interface 'Yes' is a can-claim without a link. Link privatelink-wp-endpoints-reachable-over-peering-tgw-dx ("You can access AWS PrivateLink endpoints over VPC peering, VPN, Transit Gateway, Cloud WAN, and AWS Direct Connect."), and keep the DNS caveat of claims-07 in mind.

findings.quote: | [up to 100 Gbps](../facts/transit-gateway.md#transit-gateway-quota-vpc-attachment-bandwidth) | One VPC attachment in one zone, each direction | More zones carry more traffic |
findings.evidence: The quota row (docs/vpc/latest/tgw/transit-gateway-quotas: "Bandwidth per VPC attachment per Availability Zone | Up to 100 Gbps each direction (i.e., 100 Gbps ingress and 100 Gbps egress) | Contact your Solutions Architect (SA) or Technical Account Manager (TAM) for further assistance.") supports a per-zone limit; 'More zones carry more traffic' is the writer's inference. The documented answer for more is in the same row: contact an SA or TAM.

findings.quote: | [50](../facts/vpc-endpoints.md#vpc-endpoints-quota-interface-gwlb-per-vpc) | Interface endpoints per VPC (default) |
findings.evidence: The quota is shared with Gateway Load Balancer endpoints. vpc-endpoints-quota-interface-gwlb-per-vpc, docs/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-limits-endpoints: "Interface and Gateway Load Balancer endpoints per VPC | 50 | Yes | This is a combined quota for interface endpoints and Gateway Load Balancer endpoints". Write 'Interface and Gateway Load Balancer endpoints per VPC, combined (default)'.

findings.quote: 1. **Attach.** A **transit gateway attachment** joins one VPC: you [specify one subnet from each Availability Zone](../facts/transit-gateway.md#transit-gateway-vpc-attachment-one-subnet-per-az-entry-exit) (AZ).
findings.evidence: Read alone, the step says every AZ of the VPC must have an attachment subnet, yet the Spot the bug right below depends on an attachment that leaves AZ 3 out (transit-gateway-az-without-attachment-cannot-reach: "However, only resources that reside in Availability Zones where there is a transit gateway attachment can reach the transit gateway."). Say 'one subnet in each AZ that you want to use' so the step and the exercise agree.

findings.quote: "The thing to watch is cost. A transit gateway charges per hour for each attachment, plus per gigabyte of traffic."
findings.evidence: kp4 links transit-gateway-pricing-hourly-attachment-and-data-processing, whose quote says "the amount of traffic that flows through AWS Transit Gateway", not per gigabyte. The per-GB wording is verified in transit-gateway-pricing-data-processing-per-gb-sent-to-gateway; add it to kp4.facts.

findings.quote: **Decision.** An endpoint service behind a Network Load Balancer. Peering fails: you [cannot create a VPC peering connection](../facts/vpc-peering.md#vpc-peering-no-overlap-ipv4-ipv6) between overlapping blocks.
findings.evidence: The requirement asks for the MOST secure design, but the decision argues only feasibility (overlap). The security reasons are verified and used elsewhere in the chapter: privatelink-endpoint-service-not-available-by-default ("You must add permissions that allow specific AWS principals to connect to your endpoint service.") and privatelink-wp-only-consumer-initiates ("only consumer VPCs initiate connections to the service provider VPC"). One sentence ('the bank reaches only the API, and only the bank can start a connection') makes the record answer its own question.
